content.overview: Defamation protects reputation under Article 21. Requires defamatory statement, reference to plaintiff, and publication to a third party. Both libel and slander are actionable per se in India. Governed by 3 affirmative defences: Justification by Truth, Fair Comment, and Absolute/Qualified Privilege. Governed by a 1-year limitation period.

content.study:
Topic at a glance
Defamation in tort is the wrongful publication of a false statement concerning the plaintiff which injures their reputation by lowering them in the estimation of right-thinking members of society, or exposes them to hatred, ridicule, or contempt, or causes them to be shunned or avoided. Reputation is an inherent attribute of human dignity protected as a fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution of India. In Indian law, defamation occupies a dual status: it is an actionable civil wrong in tort (remedy: unliquidated damages and injunction) and a criminal offence under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (formerly Section 499 of the Indian Penal Code).

Jurisprudential origin & definition
Winfield defines defamation as:
"Defamation is the publication of a statement which tends to lower a person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally or which tends to make them shun or avoid that person."
In Sim v. Stretch [1936] 2 All ER 1237, Lord Atkin formulated the classic objective judicial test:
"Would the words tend to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally?"
The standard is that of ordinary, right-thinking, reasonable members of the community—not hyper-sensitive individuals or a particular faction.

Libel vs Slander: English Common Law vs Indian Legal Position
Under English common law, defamation is divided into two distinct species:
1. Libel: Defamation in a permanent, visible, and tangible form (e.g. print, writing, photograph, statue, cinema film, audio-video broadcast). Under English law, libel is actionable per se (without proof of actual financial damage) and is also a criminal misdemeanour.
2. Slander: Defamation in a temporary, transitory, and spoken form (e.g. oral words, spoken insults, gestures). Under English law, slander is generally not actionable per se; the plaintiff must prove actual pecuniary loss ("special damage"), except in four recognized cases: (i) imputation of a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment, (ii) imputation of a contagious or infectious disease, (iii) imputation of unchastity to a woman (Slander of Women Act 1891), and (iv) imputation of unfitness or incompetence in any office, profession, trade, or business.

The Indian Legal Position (Senior Counsel & Academic Synthesis):
- In Criminal Law: The English common law distinction between libel and slander is completely abrogated. Under Section 356 BNS, 2023 (formerly Section 499 IPC), defamation explicitly includes words spoken or intended to be read, signs, and visible representations. Both libel and slander are criminal offences in India without requiring proof of special damage.
- In Civil Tort: Indian High Courts (e.g., Parvathi v. Mannar (1884) ILR 8 Mad 175; Narayana Sah v. Kannamma (1932)) have held that the technical English common law rule requiring proof of special damage for slander is unsuited to Indian conditions. In India, both libel and slander are actionable per se in civil tort without proving special financial damage.

The three indispensable ingredients of Civil Defamation
To maintain a civil suit for damages, the plaintiff must prove three elements:
1. The Statement Must Be Defamatory:
   - The statement must expose the plaintiff to hatred, contempt, ridicule, or financial injury, or lower their social standing.
   - Natural and Ordinary Meaning: The words are construed in their plain sense as understood by ordinary readers.
   - Innuendo: Where words are prima facie innocent or innocuous, but carry a secondary, hidden, or latent defamatory meaning to persons possessing knowledge of special extrinsic facts.
     - False Innuendo: Inherent alternative meaning derived from the text itself without extrinsic evidence.
     - True/Legal Innuendo: Meaning dependent on extrinsic facts known to specific recipients (Cassidy v. Daily Mirror Newspapers Ltd. [1929] — photo of man with young woman captioned as "engaged"; defamatory of his lawful wife who lived with him because acquaintances thought she was living in sin; Tolley v. J.S. Fry & Sons Ltd. [1931] — amateur golfer featured in chocolate advertisement implied he had compromised his amateur status for commercial gain).
2. The Statement Must Refer to the Plaintiff:
   - The plaintiff must prove that reasonable persons hearing or reading the statement would understand it as referring to them.
   - Intention is Irrelevant: In Hulton & Co. v. Jones [1910] AC 20, a newspaper published a fictional satirical piece about a churchwarden named "Artemus Jones" behaving dissolutely in France. A real barrister named Artemus Jones, of whom the author had never heard, sued. Held: The newspaper was liable; the test is not whom the writer intended to defame, but whether reasonable readers believed the words referred to the plaintiff.
   - Defamation of a Class: If a defamatory statement is directed against a broad class (e.g. "all politicians are corrupt" or "all lawyers are liars"), no individual member can maintain an action. However, an individual can sue if: (i) the class is so small and ascertainable that what is said of the class necessarily applies to every member (e.g. "all directors of X Company are fraudsters"), or (ii) the circumstances point specifically to the plaintiff.
3. The Statement Must Be Published:
   - Publication means communicating the defamatory matter to at least one third person other than the person defamed. Dictating a defamatory letter to a typist or sending an unsealed postcard constitutes publication.
   - Communications Between Spouses: Communication of defamatory matter by a husband to his wife, or vice versa, is NOT publication in law because husband and wife are regarded as one person (Wennhak v. Morgan (1888)). However, communicating defamatory matter about a spouse to a third party IS publication.
   - Unforeseen Interceptions: If a defamatory letter sent in a sealed envelope addressed to the plaintiff is opened by an inquisitive third person, there is no publication unless the defendant knew or ought to have anticipated that the envelope would be opened by a secretary or family member (Theaker v. Richardson [1962]).

The three affirmative defences in Civil Defamation
1. Justification by Truth:
   - In civil tort, absolute truth is a complete, absolute defence. The law will not permit a person to recover damages for injury to a reputation which they do not deserve.
   - Minor inaccuracies in immaterial details do not destroy the defence if the substance (sting of the charge) is substantially true (Alexander v. North Eastern Railway Co.).
   - Contrast with Criminal Defamation: Under Section 356 BNS / Section 499 IPC First Exception, truth ALONE is not a defence; the accused must prove both truth AND that the publication was for the "public good."
2. Fair Comment on a Matter of Public Interest:
   - Requirements:
     (a) The matter must be of legitimate public interest (e.g. governance, judicial proceedings, books, public performances, state administration).
     (b) It must be an expression of opinion or comment, not an assertion of fact.
     (c) The comment must be fair—an honest opinion which a fair-minded person could hold based on true facts.
     (d) The comment must be free from malicious intent (malice in fact defeats fair comment).
3. Privilege:
   - Absolute Privilege (Complete immunity; motive and malice are irrelevant):
     (a) Parliamentary proceedings: Speeches and debates in Parliament (Article 105(2)) and State Legislatures (Article 194(2)).
     (b) Judicial proceedings: Statements made by judges, advocates, parties, and witnesses in the course of judicial proceedings, provided they relate to the inquiry.
     (c) State communications: Official communications between high officers of State on state business.
   - Qualified Privilege (Immunity rebuttable by proof of express malice):
     Applies where a statement is made by a person who has a legal, moral, or social duty to communicate it, to a person who has a corresponding interest or duty to receive it (Adam v. Ward [1917]). Examples: former employer giving character reference for an employee; reporting crime to police.

Constitutional validity: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016)
In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutional validity of criminal defamation under Sections 499 and 500 IPC (now BNS s. 356). The Court held that the right to freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a) is not absolute and is reasonably restricted by Article 19(2) under the head of "defamation." The Court affirmed that an individual’s right to reputation is an integral facet of the right to life under Article 21, and that civil and criminal remedies coexist constitutionally.

Procedural & forum anchors (Senior Counsel Reference)
- Competent Forum:
  1. Civil Suit: Civil Judge (Junior or Senior Division) for unliquidated damages and permanent injunction.
  2. Criminal Prosecution: Court of Judicial Magistrate of the First Class by filing a private complaint under Section 223 BNSS (old s. 200 CrPC) for offences under Section 356 BNS.
- Limitation Period:
  - Schedule to Limitation Act, 1963:
    - Article 75: For compensation for libel — 1 year from the date when the libel is published.
    - Article 76: For compensation for slander — 1 year from the date when the words are spoken.
- Interim Injunctions & The Bonnard v. Perryman Rule:
  - In civil defamation, Indian courts strictly apply the common law rule in Bonnard v. Perryman [1891] 2 Ch 269: An interlocutory injunction to restrain publication will NOT be granted if the defendant states on affidavit that they intend to plead justification (truth) or fair comment, unless the statement is unmistakably libellous and the defence is manifestly frivolous. This safeguards free speech and prevents prior censorship.

Adversarial courtroom submissions
- Plaintiff / Complainant Submissions:
  1. The statement directly damages moral, professional, or commercial reputation.
  2. Publication was made to third parties with intent to demean or reckless indifference to truth.
  3. Rebut qualified privilege by producing evidence of personal spite, ill-will, or collateral motive (express malice).
- Defendant / Publisher Submissions:
  1. The statement is substantially true in substance and fact (justification).
  2. The publication constitutes fair comment on a matter of legitimate public concern.
  3. Occasion is cloaked with absolute or qualified privilege.
  4. Oppose interim restraint relying on the Bonnard v. Perryman doctrine.

Current-law close
Civil defamation in India enforces reputation under Article 21, while guarding free speech through the defences of justification, fair comment, and qualified privilege. Actions are subject to a strict 1-year limitation under Articles 75 and 76 of the Limitation Act.

examples.title: Example — Innuendo actionable
examples.body: A national newspaper publishes a front-page photograph of a well-known married industrialist and a glamorous model with the caption: "Mr. X announces his engagement to Ms. Y." Mr. X’s lawful wife, Mrs. X, who was living with him, sues for defamation. On the face of it, announcing an engagement is innocent. However, to acquaintances who knew Mr. X and Mrs. X were living together as husband and wife, the caption carried the true innuendo that Mrs. X was not his lawful wife but was living in immoral cohabitation. Held: The newspaper is liable for innuendo (Cassidy v. Daily Mirror Newspapers Ltd. [1929]).

examples.title: Example — Class defamation (not actionable)
examples.body: A public speaker during a heated election rally proclaims: "All lawyers in this state are blood-sucking extortionists." A practicing advocate in the state files a civil suit for ₹10 lakhs damages. Held: Where defamatory words refer to a large, indeterminate class, no individual member can sue unless there is something pointing specifically to that particular individual. The suit must be dismissed (Knupffer v. London Express Newspaper Ltd.).

examples.title: Example — Qualified privilege
examples.body: A former employer writes a confidential letter to a prospective employer who requested a reference regarding a former accountant, stating: "He was dismissed because company cash was found missing from his desk drawer." The statement was made honestly without malice. Held: The former employer had a moral and social duty to disclose the information, and the prospective employer had a reciprocal interest to receive it. The communication is protected by Qualified Privilege and is not actionable unless express malice is proved (Adam v. Ward).

hypotheticals.question: Should the civil court grant an interim injunction restraining publication of the news article? How do Indian courts apply the rule in Bonnard v. Perryman?
hypotheticals.analysis:
In suits for defamation, the grant of an ex-parte or interlocutory injunction restraining publication requires extreme judicial caution because it encroaches directly upon freedom of the press under Article 19(1)(a).
Under the landmark principle of Bonnard v. Perryman [1891] 2 Ch 269, reaffirmed by the Supreme Court of India in Bloomberg Television Production Services India v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd. (2024), courts will not grant an interlocutory injunction to restrain alleged defamation if the defendant asserts an intention to justify the statement (plead truth) or plead fair comment, unless the court is satisfied that the statement is unmistakably defamatory and that no reasonable jury or court could find the defence established.
Here, The Probe India has placed prima facie laboratory test reports and official audit documents on record and undertaken under oath to plead truth and fair comment on a matter of grave public safety (flyover stability). Granting a prior restraint would stifle investigative journalism and public awareness.
Consequently, the application for an interim gag order must be rejected. The plaintiff’s remedy lies in claiming damages at trial if the allegations are ultimately proved false.

rows.right: Codified statutory offence under Section 356 BNS, 2023

rows.right: Truth alone is NOT enough; must be coupled with "public good" (Exception 1)

misconceptions.trap: Believing that in India, spoken slander requires proof of special monetary damage.
misconceptions.correction: In India, both libel and slander are actionable per se in civil tort without requiring proof of special financial damage (Parvathi v. Mannar). Furthermore, spoken words are fully criminalized under BNS Section 356.

misconceptions.trap: Assuming a newspaper can be automatically restrained from publishing an investigative story by filing a defamation suit.
misconceptions.correction: Under the Bonnard v. Perryman rule, if the media defendant undertakes to plead truth and fair comment on public interest, courts will not grant pre-trial gag orders, preserving freedom of speech under Article 19(1)(a).

cases.name: Sim v. Stretch
cases.holding: Formulated the standard judicial test for defamatory statements: "Would the words tend to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally?"
cases.relevance: The foundational objective test for determining whether words are capable of a defamatory meaning.

cases.name: Cassidy v. Daily Mirror Newspapers Ltd.
cases.holding: Held that publication of an apparently innocent photograph of a man and woman announcing their engagement was actionable in innuendo by the man’s lawful wife, because acquaintances would reasonably infer she was living with him as an unmarried mistress.
cases.relevance: The leading common law authority on the doctrine of Innuendo in defamation.

cases.name: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India
cases.holding: Upheld the constitutional validity of criminal defamation under Sections 499 and 500 IPC (now BNS s. 356). Ruled that the right to reputation is an integral facet of Article 21 and a reasonable restriction on Article 19(1)(a) free speech.
cases.relevance: Landmark constitutional precedent balancing freedom of speech against the right to reputation.

cases.name: Bloomberg Television v. Zee Entertainment Enterprises Ltd.
cases.citation: 2024 SCC OnLine SC 426 (Supreme Court of India)
cases.holding: Reaffirmed the Bonnard v. Perryman principle in India. Pre-trial ex-parte injunctions against media publications must not be granted mechanically; courts must rigorously assess whether the defendant has a plausible defence of truth or fair comment.
cases.relevance: Latest Supreme Court authority curbing pre-publication gag orders in corporate defamation suits.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Define the tort of Defamation. What are its essential ingredients? Explain the doctrine of Innuendo with the aid of decided cases.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Introduction and Definition
Defamation in tort is the publication of a false and unprivileged statement concerning the plaintiff which injures their reputation.
Winfield defines defamation as:
"The publication of a statement which tends to lower a person in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally or which tends to make them shun or avoid that person."
In Sim v. Stretch [1936], Lord Atkin formulated the classic test:
"Would the words tend to lower the plaintiff in the estimation of right-thinking members of society generally?"

### 2. Essential Ingredients of Defamation
To succeed in a civil action for defamation, the plaintiff must prove three elements:

#### A. The Statement Must Be Defamatory
The statement must be calculated to expose the plaintiff to hatred, contempt, ridicule, or cause them to be shunned. The standard is objective, judged by the impact on ordinary, sensible members of the community.

#### B. The Statement Must Refer to the Plaintiff
The plaintiff must establish that reasonable persons acquainted with them would understand the statement as referring to the plaintiff.
In Hulton & Co. v. Jones [1910] AC 20, an author wrote a fictional article describing the immoral behavior of a fictional person named "Artemus Jones." A real barrister of that name sued. The House of Lords held that the defendant's intention was immaterial; since reasonable people believed the article referred to the real Artemus Jones, the newspaper was held liable.

#### C. The Statement Must Be Published
Publication means communicating the defamatory matter to at least one person other than the plaintiff.
- Spouses: Communication between husband and wife is not publication (Wennhak v. Morgan). However, a third party communicating defamatory remarks to a spouse constitutes publication.

### 3. The Doctrine of Innuendo
Sometimes words which are harmless, innocent, or even complimentary on their face carry a concealed defamatory meaning because of extrinsic facts known to the recipients. This hidden defamatory imputation is called an **Innuendo**.
Innuendos are of two types:
1. False Innuendo: An inherent secondary meaning which arises naturally from the words themselves (reading between the lines).
2. True (Legal) Innuendo: A hidden defamatory meaning which arises only when read in conjunction with special extrinsic facts known to specific persons.

#### Landmark Case on Innuendo:
- Cassidy v. Daily Mirror Newspapers Ltd. [1929] 2 KB 331:
  The defendant newspaper published a photograph of Mr. Corrigan and a young woman, captioning it: "Mr. Corrigan and Miss X, whose engagement has been announced." The plaintiff, Mrs. Corrigan (Cassidy), was Mr. Corrigan’s lawful wife and lived with him.
  To the general public, the announcement was harmless. But to neighbours and friends who knew that Mrs. Cassidy was living with Mr. Corrigan, the statement implied by innuendo that she was not his lawful wife but was living in immoral concubinage. The Court of Appeal held the newspaper liable for defamation.

- Tolley v. J.S. Fry & Sons Ltd. [1931] AC 333:
  An amateur golf champion was depicted in a caricature with a packet of the defendant's chocolate sticking out of his pocket. Held: The innuendo was that he had compromised his amateur status by accepting advertising remuneration, which was defamatory in the golfing community.

### 4. Conclusion
Defamation safeguards reputation as a property of character. Where words do not defame directly, the doctrine of innuendo ensures that disguised or veiled attacks on reputation remain actionable under the law of torts.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Critically examine the defences available in a civil suit for Defamation. Distinguish between Civil Defamation and Criminal Defamation under Indian law, and discuss the constitutional reconciliation between Article 19(1)(a) and Article 21 in Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India.
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
### 1. Abstract & Introduction
Defamation represents the perpetual legal battleground between two fundamental constitutional values: the individual's right to reputation as a component of personal dignity under Article 21, and the freedom of speech and expression guaranteed under Article 19(1)(a). Indian jurisprudence accommodates both private law remedies in tort (compensatory damages and injunctions) and public penal sanctions under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. This answer analyzes the affirmative defences in civil tort, contrasts civil and criminal regimes, and evaluates the constitutional balance struck by the Supreme Court.

### 2. Defences Available in Civil Defamation
Under the law of torts, a defendant who has published defamatory matter may escape liability by establishing one of three established affirmative defences:

#### A. Justification by Truth
1. Absolute Truth is a Complete Defence:
   In civil law, the truth of the defamatory imputation is an absolute shield. The law will not permit a person to recover damages for injury to a character they do not possess.
2. Substantial Truth Suffices:
   The defendant is not required to prove the literal truth of every trivial detail; it is sufficient if the "substance or sting of the charge" is justified (Alexander v. North Eastern Railway Co., 1865).
3. Contrast with Criminal Law:
   Under civil tort, malice is irrelevant if the statement is true. Under criminal law (Exception 1 to BNS s. 356 / IPC s. 499), truth ALONE is no defence; the accused must prove both truth AND that the publication was for the "public good."

#### B. Fair Comment on a Matter of Public Interest
To succeed in the defence of fair comment, four elements must concur:
1. Public Interest: The subject matter commented upon must be of legitimate public concern (e.g. government policy, administration of justice, public conduct of officials, published literature, theatrical works).
2. Comment, Not Statement of Fact: The words must be an expression of opinion, deduction, or criticism. If facts are stated, they must be true.
3. Fair and Honest: The comment must be an honest expression of opinion which a fair-minded person could form on the proved facts.
4. Absence of Malice: The defence of fair comment is immediately defeated if the plaintiff proves that the defendant was actuated by express malice, personal spite, or ill-will.

#### C. Privilege
The law recognizes that on certain occasions, the public interest in complete freedom of communication outweighs the individual's interest in reputation. Privilege is of two kinds:
1. Absolute Privilege (Complete Immunity; Malice Irrelevant):
   - Parliamentary Proceedings: Speeches, reports, and votes in Parliament (Article 105(2)) and State Legislatures (Article 194(2)).
   - Judicial Proceedings: Statements made by judges, counsel, parties, and witnesses in court touching the matter in issue.
   - State Communications: Official communications between high officers of State.
2. Qualified Privilege (Immunity Conditional on Absence of Malice):
   - Arises where a statement is made by a person who has a legal, social, or moral duty to make it, to a recipient who has a corresponding interest or duty to receive it (Adam v. Ward [1917]).
   - Examples: An employer providing a character reference for an employee; a citizen reporting suspected crime to a police officer.
   - Effect of Malice: Qualified privilege is destroyed if the plaintiff proves express malice (collateral spite or knowledge of falsity).

### 3. Comparative Matrix: Civil vs Criminal Defamation in India
| Dimension | Civil Defamation (Tort) | Criminal Defamation (BNS s. 356 / IPC s. 499) |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of Proceeding | Private action between citizens | State/Private prosecution for penal sanction |
| Primary Remedy | Unliquidated monetary damages & injunction | Imprisonment up to 2 years, fine, or community service |
| Defence of Truth | Absolute truth is a complete defence per se | Truth MUST be coupled with "public good" |
| Libel vs Slander | Both actionable per se in India | Both punishable equally as criminal offences |
| Standard of Proof | Preponderance of probabilities | Beyond reasonable doubt |
| Limitation Period | 1 year (Articles 75 & 76 Limitation Act) | 3 years (Section 468 CrPC / BNSS s. 514) |

### 4. Constitutional Reconciliation: Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016)
In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016) 7 SCC 221, petitioners challenged the constitutional validity of Sections 499 and 500 IPC, arguing that criminalizing defamation exerted a "chilling effect" on free speech and democratic dissent under Article 19(1)(a).
A two-judge bench of the Supreme Court dismissed the challenge and upheld criminal defamation:
1. Reputation as an Article 21 Right:
   The Court held that the right to reputation is not merely a common law right, but an essential component of personal liberty and human dignity guaranteed under Article 21.
2. Permissible Restriction under Article 19(2):
   Article 19(2) expressly mentions "defamation" as a ground for imposing reasonable restrictions on speech. The Court held that criminal defamation is proportionate and serves to protect social peace and individual dignity.
3. Coexistence of Remedies:
   The Court affirmed that civil and criminal remedies operate in distinct spheres: civil law repairs private reputation through damages, while criminal law vindicates public order and deters malicious character assassination.

### 5. Prior Restraint and the Bonnard v. Perryman Doctrine
In commercial and political defamation, plaintiffs frequently seek ex-parte interim injunctions to gag publication. In Bloomberg Television v. Zee Entertainment (2024), the Supreme Court reiterated the historic rule in Bonnard v. Perryman [1891]:
Interim injunctions restraining publication must not be granted if the defendant intends to plead justification or fair comment at trial. Prior censorship strikes at the core of a free press and can only be justified where the libel is indisputably false and undefendable.

### 6. Conclusion
The law of defamation in India successfully synthesizes common law tort principles with constitutional safeguards. While Article 21 demands that an individual's hard-earned reputation be vigorously shielded, the defences of truth, fair comment, and the Bonnard v. Perryman restraint ensure that public accountability and constitutional free expression remain uncompromised.
questionsAndAnswers.explanation: Scoring Rubric: Allocate 4 marks for the three defences in civil tort (justification, fair comment, absolute/qualified privilege), 4 marks for the comparison matrix between civil and criminal defamation, 5 marks for Subramanian Swamy analysis (Art 19(1)(a) vs Art 21), and 3 marks for Bonnard v. Perryman rule and conclusion.

revisionPoints: Definition: Statement lowering plaintiff in estimation of right-thinking members of society (Sim v. Stretch).
Libel (permanent) vs Slander (transitory): In India, both are actionable per se in civil tort (Parvathi v. Mannar) and criminalized under Section 356 BNS.
Three ingredients: Defamatory statement, referring to plaintiff (Hulton v. Jones), and published to a third party.
Innuendo: Statement innocent on its face but defamatory due to extrinsic facts (Cassidy v. Daily Mirror, Tolley v. Fry).
Defences: Justification by Truth (absolute in civil tort), Fair Comment on public interest, and Absolute/Qualified Privilege.
Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India (2016): Criminal defamation upheld; right to reputation is part of Article 21.
Bonnard v. Perryman / Bloomberg v. Zee (2024): Pre-trial injunctions denied if defendant intends to plead truth or fair comment.
Limitation: 1 year under Articles 75 and 76 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
examTips: Remember: In civil tort, truth alone is an absolute defence; in criminal law under BNS s. 356, truth must be accompanied by "public good".
Quote Lord Atkin’s test in Sim v. Stretch in all university exam answers.
Cite Bloomberg Television v. Zee Entertainment (2024) to demonstrate cutting-edge knowledge on interim injunctions in defamation.

Granting a prior restraint would stifle investigative journalism and public awareness.
Consequently, the application for an interim gag order must be rejected. The plaintiff’s remedy lies in claiming damages at trial if the allegations are ultimately proved false.
keyTakeaways: Defamation protects reputation under Article 21. Requires defamatory statement, reference to plaintiff, and publication to a third party. Both libel and slander are actionable per se in India. Governed by 3 affirmative defences: Justification by Truth, Fair Comment, and Absolute/Qualified Privilege. Governed by a 1-year limitation period.
